# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# The Letters of Harrow Bend

In the town of Harrow Bend, the post office has not delivered a letter in forty-one years, and nobody has ever asked it to stop trying.

The building sits at the end of Mill Street, a narrow brick box with a flag that hangs limp in still weather. Inside, a counter runs the width of the room, polished by elbows. Behind it are rows of wooden pigeonholes, each labeled in faded black ink with the name of a place: *Lisbon. Tacoma. Ashgrove. Kyiv. Nowhere Road. The Coast.* The railway that once connected Harrow Bend to the rest of the world was torn up in the winter of the flood, and the last mail train pulled out with its brakes screaming. Nobody remembers who the last passenger was. Everyone remembers the sound.

Ruth Calloway has run the post office since she was twenty-six. She is now seventy-three, and she has the particular stillness of someone who has spent most of her life listening for footsteps that don't come.

People still bring her letters. That is the strange part, and Ruth has stopped trying to explain it to the visitors from the county, who sometimes come asking about the building's status and leave with their questions unanswered. The letters arrive at odd hours: tucked under the door, pushed through the brass slot, left on the counter with a stone on top so the wind won't take them. Some are sealed. Some are addressed in careful handwriting to people who are dead. Some are addressed to people who never lived in Harrow Bend at all, to cities the writers have only seen on television, to streets that may not exist anymore.

Ruth stamps every one. She has a rubber stamp that reads *POSTED*, and the ink has gone grey from use. She sorts each letter into the pigeonhole that matches its destination, and when a letter has no destination she puts it in the drawer marked *Return to Sender*, which is the largest drawer in the building.

Nobody has ever asked for their letter back.

---

On a Thursday in late October, a boy of about nine came in with his coat buttoned wrong and an envelope clenched in both hands. He didn't go to the counter. He stood by the door, breathing hard, as if he had run the whole way from the school.

"Are you the postmistress?" he asked.

"I am," Ruth said. "Come here where I can see you. You're letting the cold in."

He crossed the room slowly. He had a round face and a cowlick that would not lie down, and when he set the envelope on the counter, he kept one finger on it, as though it might try to leave.

It was addressed in large, uneven capitals: *DAD. THE TRAIN STATION. PLEASE COME BACK.*

"Where's your father, love?" Ruth asked gently.

"He went on the train," the boy said. "Last spring. He said he'd send a postcard from the city. He said I'd get it in a week." He swallowed. "I didn't get it."

Ruth had been expecting many things in forty-one years. She had not been expecting this, and for a moment she simply looked at the envelope, at the press of the boy's small finger against the paper.

"Mail doesn't come in here anymore," the boy said, carefully, as if he were being fair to her. "I know that. Everybody knows that. But my mum said if you write it down and put it somewhere, it doesn't just disappear. So I wrote it down."

"Your mum's a wise woman," Ruth said.

"She's not. She cries in the car."

Ruth almost laughed, and then she didn't, because the boy's face had crumpled for half a second before he forced it straight again. She knew that expression. She had worn it herself, for a long time, at this same counter.

"What's your name?"

"Teodor."

"Teodor. Do you know what happens to letters that come into this office?"

He shook his head.

"They go into the back room," she said. "Where they wait. And they don't wait for a train, or a truck, or a plane. They wait because somebody took the trouble to write them. That's the whole job, really. Making sure something made with care isn't thrown away."

"Will he get it?"

Ruth looked at the capitals again. *PLEASE COME BACK.* She thought about how many people had stood where Teodor was standing, asking that same question with their eyes if not with their mouths. She thought about the drawer marked *Return to Sender* and how she had never once opened it to check whether anything had been answered.

"I don't know," she said honestly. "But I'll put it in the right pocket. The one for the station. And I'll stamp it, and I'll keep it safe. Whatever happens, it won't be lost."

Teodor considered this with the seriousness of a child who has been lied to often enough to recognize the difference between comfort and truth.

"Okay," he said at last.

She took the envelope, turned it over, and pressed the stamp onto the back. *POSTED.* The ink came out grey and a little uneven, the way it always did. Then she slid it into the pigeonhole labeled *Station*, which was not a real destination, which had not been a real destination for forty-one years.

Teodor watched it go in. Something in his shoulders loosened.

"Can I see the back room?" he asked.

"Not today," Ruth said. "But come back on Thursday. I'll show you the stamp."

---

After he left, the room was quiet except for the tick of the old radiator. Ruth stood at the counter for a long time. Then she pulled a sheet of paper from the drawer beneath the scale, uncapped her pen, and began to write.

*To whoever is keeping the trains running,* she wrote, and then crossed it out, because it was foolish, and then wrote it again, because it was true.

She wrote about the flood and the bridge and the sound the brakes had made. She wrote about her mother, who had sent a letter every week from the hospital in the city until the week she didn't. She wrote about the first postcard she ever stamped, when she was twenty-six and certain she would be gone in a year. She wrote that she had stayed, and that staying had not been the same as giving up, though for a long time she had believed it was.

She wrote, finally, a return address. She stopped with the pen above the paper, then wrote it slowly, in her best hand: *Ruth Calloway, Post Office, Mill Street, Harrow Bend.*

She folded the letter, sealed it, and held it for a moment in her palm. It weighed almost nothing.

Then she walked to the drawer marked *Return to Sender*, slid it open, and placed her letter inside, on top of the others.

She had been waiting her whole life for someone to come to the counter and tell her where she belonged. It occurred to her now, standing in the grey October light with the radiator ticking and a boy's uneven capitals waiting in the back room, that she had been the one holding the stamp all along.

She closed the drawer gently, the way you'd close a door on someone sleeping, and went to lock up for the night.

Outside, the flag stirred, just slightly, as if a train were somewhere far off, coming slowly around the bend.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a small-town post office and a quiet emotional revelation.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender and restrained, letting grief emerge through ordinary gestures: a boy keeping one finger on an envelope, Ruth stamping a letter she cannot deliver, the old radiator ticking in the silence. Its central pathos is the ache of waiting—for an absent father, a lost mother, a vanished railway, or a place to belong. The story invites the reader to treat care itself as meaningful even when it cannot guarantee reunion or an answer.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds letters, destinations that no longer exist, and the rituals people use to keep loss from becoming disappearance. Its moral emphasis is gentle rather than triumphant: Ruth does not promise the boy that his father will return, but she can promise not to throw away what he made with care. The ending turns that same act of preservation toward Ruth’s own buried sense of belonging.

## Evidence line
> She had been waiting her whole life for someone to come to the counter and tell her where she belonged.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained motifs of waiting, grief, and small acts of care give the piece a distinctive, coherent emotional center.
